• Bc 26.60 from TDM 15.3: These others, born in the triple heaven through meritorious deeds,
are intensely consumed by the fire of sensual passion as if by a physical flame.
For these beings, whose splendor has been destroyed, fall down still unsated by sense-objects— wearing withered garlands, dejected, and with eyes turned upward.
There,
these Apsarases catch hold of their beloved one as he falls helpless by the hem of his garment with their hands, and with tender glances from their hearts.
From their celestial chariots, they gazed piteously at their beloveds falling;
with their bodies bent down by their ornaments, they seemed as if they themselves were falling to the earth.
These other women, deprived of their beloveds and with their ornaments and garlands disarrayed,
follow after them with eyes flickering with affection, consumed by the heat of grief.
Striking their breasts with their hands as their lovers fell away,
the hosts of *apsarases* displayed distress, like that of a great family in ruin.
"Alas, Caitraratha! Alas, the pond! Alas, Mandākinī! Alas, my beloved!"—thus lamenting, the denizens of heaven indeed fall to the earth.
Fie on this heaven, attained through manifold deeds, which is unstable and impermanent!
Such is the suffering caused by separation that is experienced here.
Oh, how truly the nature of decay prevails especially among the world!
For even having attained dispassion, others fall from heaven.
With their minds resolved that "this place is eternal," they did not perceive the true nature of this world to be such as it is.
O King,
he whose nature is action has action as his source.
Knowing that the world is dependent on karma and partakes in the ripening of karma, abide by the power of karma and practice that very action which would be beneficial.
Having reflected upon and investigated the true nature of the world,
one realizes that for a man, virtuous action is indeed his only true friend; there is no other.
Even after abandoning everything along with their karma, they must go forth alone, without support.
The world of living beings goes to the realm of animals, the human world, hell, or heaven, depending upon their karma.
With craving as its cause, the world performs manifold karma, which is threefold and of three origins.
Therefore, to the best of one's ability, for the sake of liberating speech and body, and for the sake of purifying action—
Exert yourself for the concentration of the mind;
this is your own task, as well as the task of others.
Therefore, since the world of living beings is impermanent...
While the engagement with sense objects flickers like lightning,
you ought not to enjoy fruits through unrighteousness while standing at the very tip of Death’s hand.
Then, seeing Ānanda thus with a mind afflicted by grief, [the Blessed One spoke].
The Lord, the best among those who know reality, spoke, consoling him with the truth.
Having understood the nature of the world, do not give way to grief or joy;
such are conditioned phenomena, and this entire world is subject to destruction.
I have already told you before that for living beings who delight in dualities,
there is separation from all that is dear; therefore, let craving be completely eradicated.
For it is not possible to obtain that which has been born, conditioned, and unstable;
since it has arisen dependently and lacks autonomy, how could it ever become eternal for me?
If the existent were eternal, there would be no fluctuating activity;
then what need would there be for liberation? Therefore, it is held that [the existent] is subject to cessation.
Or rather, what does either you or anyone else hope for from me,
since this exertion of yours has arisen from the desire to be separated from me?
The entire path has been taught by me to you and laid bare;
let it be understood that for the Buddhas there is no "teacher’s fist" [of withheld knowledge].
Whether I remain or have attained peace, this alone is the task: what purpose do you have with my physical body? For the Tathāgatas are the Dharma-body.
Therefore, now that I have passed away, you must always wander as islands unto yourselves and as islands of the Dharma, filled with spiritual urgency and dedicated to that goal.
"...by means of the lamps of the self... by means of the lamps of the Dharma" (Buddhacarita 24.21):
"Those who have themselves as their island should be known as such—intent upon that [island] and firm in their valor."
Free from the pairs of opposites, they possess wholesome qualities and their intellects are not dependent on others.
Furthermore, those who possess knowledge and are wise should be known as islands of Dharma;
with their blazing wisdom, they destroy darkness as if with a lamp.
There are four objects of observation for the attainment of those who seek the highest good:
the body, sensation, the mind, and selflessness itself.
Seeing that the body is covered with skin, bone, blood, sinews, flesh, phlegm, and so forth,
and is thus impure, one indeed does not take delight in the physical frame.
As he perceives that sensations, which arise through various conditions,
are in every way nothing but suffering, his perception of them as pleasant is abandoned.
For one who perceives the arising, the persistence, and indeed the passing away of the mind,
the grasping at permanence ceases as the mind becomes tranquil.
For one who perceives the aggregates as having arisen from conditions,
the grasping at a self— which is the producer of the notion of "I"— does not arise.
Having thus established mindfulness upon these four subjects,
this indeed is the one-way path for the cessation of sufferings.
For those who shall dwell here now, and after my passing,
will attain the supreme, imperishable state of ultimate bliss.
Thus the Guide related that very story for the sake of Ānanda;
and having heard it, the Licchavis, moved by his state of mind, arrived there swiftly.
Out of love and devotion for the Sage, their minds were overcome by grief;
they set aside all other concerns and, in their agitation, cast off their royal splendors.
Having prostrated, those who desired to enter [the city] sat down before the Teacher;
and perceiving that they wished to speak, the Sage indeed addressed these words to them.
This disposition of yours directed toward me— I recognize all of this;
yet, because of your dejection, they appear to me today as if they were someone else.
And in every way, by your remaining thus even amidst glorious pleasures,
this persistent attachment of yours has manifested a profound mastery of the Dharma.
But if you have heard from me anything that is to be known, and if you have understood it at all,
then do not grieve regarding my peace; go and remain steadfast in your own state.
Conditioned phenomena are impermanent, unstable, and subject to change;
they are devoid of essence and unreliable, for there is no state whatsoever that remains constant.
Vasiṣṭha, Atri, and others, as well as those who were perpetual celibates,
have all fallen under the power of Time; such is the inexhaustible nature of worldly existence.
Māndhātṛ, the sustainer of the earth; Vasu, equal to Śakra;
then Nābhāga, who possessed great enjoyments; and Saṃbhūta, who was compassionate toward all beings.
Then Yayāti, Śayyāti, Suratha, Bhagīratha, Purukutsa, the king Puru, Rāma, Rāji, Aja, and Raja.
These and many other great-souled royal sages,
equal to Mahendra, have perished; for nothing that is indestructible exists.
When the sun has fallen from its station, the Vasus depart for the earth;
hundreds of Indras have passed away, for nothing whatsoever is eternal.
And those others who were perfectly awakened ones, they too entered nirvana,
having provided light for the world like lamps when their oil is exhausted.
And those other Tathāgatas who have perfected themselves and will likewise appear—
they too shall attain final nirvāṇa, like a fire when its fuel is consumed.
Therefore, desiring liberation, I too shall depart from this refuge;
for there is no reason for me to carry this worthless thing known as a body.
A destroyer of Dharma and a ruin of fame.
Anger is the enemy of beauty and the fire of the heart; one must not grant it any scope,
for there is no other foe of virtues like it.
Nothing is difficult to achieve through valor.
Therefore, strive without laying down your burden;
for even a soft stream of water, when flowing constantly over time, pierces a surface of rock.

Buddhacarita 26.60 Then, having seen that the king was distressed by grief, the son of Aṃśumat spoke these words to him, whose mind was fixed on the path of dharma: “Do not grieve, O King, for this is the way of all beings; for even the gods do not escape the power of time.”
